relationship: Achish's war summons and David's later position in the procession

relationship: Achish's promised bodyguard appointment and his later favourable assessment
rationale: Achish responds to David's unspecified undertaking by promising him the chief bodyguard position; he later calls David upright and good in his eyes, preserving the promise as his speech rather than claiming that the appointment was carried out.

relationship: Same-chapter successive reported perceptions and Saul's recognition
rationale: The woman first reports gods coming up from the earth; when asked what she perceived, she describes a standing man in a double cloak and Saul recognises Samuel, retaining the plural and singular wording and the distinct perceivers.

relationship: Double-cloak descriptions in the two Saul-and-Samuel encounters

relationship: The Lord's departure in Samuel's speech and the earlier Spirit notice
rationale: Samuel says the Lord has departed from Saul; the earlier narrative specifically says the Lord's Spirit departed from Saul, preserving the two subjects as actually supplied and the earlier account's additional evil-spirit statement.

relationship: The kingdom-tearing announcement expressly recalls Samuel's earlier word
rationale: Samuel now says the Lord acts as He spoke through him and will give the kingdom to the neighbour David; the earlier oracle says the kingdom has been torn from Saul's hand and will be given to a better neighbour, whose name is supplied in the later speech.

relationship: The kingdom's transfer to David in speech and retrospective assessment
rationale: Samuel announces that the kingdom will be taken from Saul and given to David; Chronicles says the Lord turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse, matching that named transfer while retaining its additional judgment explanation.

relationship: Disobedience concerning Amalek recalls the earlier mission and rebuke
rationale: Samuel now grounds the judgment in Saul's failure to hear the Lord and carry out His anger against Amalek; the earlier rebuke names that mission against Amalek and asks why Saul did not hear the Lord's voice but rushed to the spoils.

relationship: Announced defeat and death followed by the battle's narrated outcome

relationship: Same-chapter lack of food and strength answered by the woman's food appeal

relationship: Same-chapter the woman's stated compliance refers to the earlier request

relationship: Same-chapter the appeal to eat before travelling and the reported meal and departure

relationship: Same-chapter initial unwillingness and eventual response to the food appeal

relationship: Same-chapter announced bread provision specified as heifer and unleavened cakes

relationship: Same-chapter eating and departing answer the request to eat before the journey

relationship: Same-chapter the foreign muster and the chapter's separated departures

relationship: David's place with Achish follows the explicit command to accompany him

relationship: Achish's defence repeats his earlier trust in David

relationship: Same-chapter the generals' objection and Achish's return order
rationale: The generals demand David's removal because they fear a plot against the camp; Achish then distinguishes his own favourable view from the satraps' view and orders David to return in peace, giving the specific response to their objection.

relationship: The generals expressly repeat the Saul-and-David victory refrain

relationship: David identified by the same refrain in two foreign-court conversations
rationale: The generals invoke the song naming Saul's thousands and David's tens of thousands; Achish's servants had previously identified David with that same quoted refrain, connecting the particular remembered words and named man.

relationship: Same-chapter Achish's favourable assessment repeated to a different audience
rationale: Achish tells David he has found no evil in him and calls him good in his eyes; his earlier answer to the generals likewise says he has found nothing against him, retaining both speeches as his assessments and their different audiences.

relationship: Same-chapter commanded return and the actual departure apart from Israel's attackers
rationale: Achish commands David to return peacefully; the ending reports David and his men leaving to guard the foreigners' land while the foreigners go to war against Israel, preserving both stated destinations and actions.

relationship: Same-chapter David's exclusion question answered by Achish

relationship: Same-chapter Achish reports the generals' earlier refusal of David's participation

relationship: Same-chapter early-departure instruction and performance
rationale: Achish tells David and the accompanying servants to rise early and depart; David and his men then rise early and leave, without assigning an additional identity to the master mentioned in the instruction.

relationship: The separated departure leads into David's return to Ziklag
rationale: After David and his men leave to guard the foreigners' land while the foreigners attack Israel, the next account places his company entering Ziklag on the third day and finding the aftermath of Amalek's attack, without calculating an unreported calendar date.

relationship: Ziklag's destruction concerns the town previously given to David
rationale: David returns to find Ziklag struck and burned by Amalek; the earlier account identifies Ziklag as the town Achish gave him, supplying its specific connection with David's company and preserving the earlier king-of-Judea statement.

relationship: Same-chapter the Ziklag raid recounted by the Egyptian slave
rationale: The narrator names Amalek's attack and burning of Ziklag; the youth identifies his master as an Amalekite and says his group burned Ziklag, connecting the explicit city and action while preserving Cholthi and Cheloub as supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter all taken captive and the later all-recovered report
rationale: The raid takes small and great captive without killing man or woman; the recovery notice says nothing small or great, including sons and daughters and possessions, was missing, linking the particular capture and restoration summaries.

relationship: Same-chapter the discovered burned city follows the narrated raid
rationale: David's company finds the city burned and families captive; the opening already names Amalek's attack on Ziklag and its burning, supplying the narrated cause of the state they discover.

relationship: Same-chapter exhausted grief and David's later stated strengthening
rationale: The company weeps until it has no strength to weep; the later anguish over sons and daughters includes threats against David and the statement that he was strengthened in the Lord, preserving the particular weakness-and-strength contrast without claiming grief vanished.

relationship: The captured pair of David's wives recalls their earlier marriage notices
rationale: Ahinoam and Abigail are named as David's two captured wives; the earlier notices report Abigail becoming his wife and Ahinoam from Jezreel also being his wife, retaining the later supplied designation of Abigail as Nabal's wife.

relationship: David strengthened in the Lord in two specified crises
rationale: Amid the threatened stoning David is strengthened in the Lord his God; earlier Jonathan strengthens David's hands in the Lord while Saul seeks him, preserving the different crisis and the earlier human agent.

relationship: David's repeated request to Abiathar the priest for the ephoud
rationale: David tells Abiathar to bring the ephoud before the pursuit inquiry; in the earlier Keilah danger he likewise tells Abiathar the priest to bring the Lord's ephoud, matching the named priest and particular preparation without resolving differing ancestral forms elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter promised rescue and the explicit full recovery
rationale: The answer to David's inquiry promises pursuit, overtaking and rescue; the later account says he recovered everything Amalek took, rescued both wives and brought back all the people and possessions, recording the specific promised outcome.

relationship: Same-chapter the six hundred divided into pursuing and remaining groups
rationale: Six hundred accompany David to the Bosor torrent; the following unit specifies four hundred pursuing and two hundred remaining, accounting for the stated group's division without importing a different earlier troop total.

relationship: Same-chapter the two hundred at Bosor later rejoined
rationale: Two hundred remain beyond the Bosor torrent while four hundred pursue; the later return explicitly identifies the two hundred seated at Bosor as too weak to follow, explaining that particular remaining group in the later wording.

relationship: Same-chapter bread and water followed by further food and the stated lack
rationale: The Egyptian receives bread and water; the next unit adds fruit cake and says his spirit settled after three days without bread or water, connecting the specified provisions and stated deprivation without a medical interpretation.

relationship: Same-chapter the deprivation notice explains the preceding food and water gift
rationale: The youth eats fruit cake and his spirit settles after three days without bread or water; the preceding encounter supplies bread and water given to that Egyptian, retaining the separate food details and the stated duration.

relationship: Same-chapter the abandoned slave's ownership and his later return-to-master condition
rationale: The youth identifies himself as an Amalekite man's slave abandoned during illness; his later offer to guide David requires that he not be killed or handed back to his master, linking the stated ownership with his precise requested protection.

relationship: Same-chapter the youth's Ziklag-burning report recalls the opening raid notice
rationale: The youth reports that his group burned Ziklag after attacks on the named southern regions; the opening narration says Amalek struck and burned Ziklag, connecting the explicitly shared city and action without renaming Cholthi or Cheloub.

relationship: Same-chapter requested guidance and the actual descent to the raiders
rationale: David asks the youth to guide him and the youth offers conditional help; the next unit says he took him down to the scattered raiders, without inserting an unreported oath or answer from David.

relationship: Same-chapter raiders' celebration contrasted with the company's grief
rationale: The raiders eat, drink and celebrate over great spoils; David's earlier company finds its families captive and weeps until it has no strength to weep, giving the particular contrasting reactions within the same raid-and-recovery account.

relationship: Same-chapter the attack followed by restoration of the captured people and goods
rationale: David strikes the raiders, with four hundred camel-riding youths escaping; the following recovery summary restores what Amalek took, distinguishing those escaped attackers from the rescued captives and possessions.

relationship: Same-chapter both rescued wives are the pair earlier named as captive
rationale: The recovery specifically includes both David's wives; the earlier loss notice names the captured pair Ahinoam and Abigail, supplying the exact household reference behind that rescue statement.

relationship: Same-chapter nothing missing reverses the small-and-great captivity summary
rationale: The final recovery leaves nothing small or great missing, including sons and daughters; the raid notice had taken small and great captive without killing man or woman, connecting those particular comprehensive summaries.

relationship: Same-chapter attributed spoils and the later announced distribution
rationale: The flocks and herds are led ahead and the spoils are called David's spoils; David later sends some spoils to Judah's elders and his neighbours as spoils of the Lord's enemies, retaining the different attribution language and his specific act of distribution.

relationship: Same-chapter the reunited two hundred recall the earlier division at Bosor
rationale: David returns to the two hundred unable to follow and seated at Bosor; the earlier division had left two hundred there while four hundred pursued, matching the named torrent and counted group rather than an unrelated troop number.

relationship: Same-chapter denying a share to the nonpursuers answered by equal sharing
rationale: The pestilent and evil warriors would give the nonpursuers only their wives and children; David's response gives equal shares to the fighter and equipment keeper, directly rejecting their proposed exclusion from spoils.

relationship: Same-chapter David's divine-credit speech follows the favourable pursuit oracle
rationale: David credits the Lord with giving, guarding and delivering the raiding band; the earlier answer to his inquiry promised pursuit, overtaking and rescue, connecting the specific oracle with his later attribution without adding an unstated promise about casualties.

relationship: Spoils allotted beyond the combatants under differently stated rules
rationale: David gives the equipment keeper the same share as the warrior; Numbers divides spoils between warriors and the whole congregation, providing a related inclusion of those outside the battle while retaining the distinct groups and allocation wording.

relationship: Same-chapter the standing rule refers to the stated equal-share decision
rationale: The notice makes this a command and rule for Israel from that day; the preceding decision states equal shares for the warrior and equipment keeper, supplying the actual content of the rule rather than a new unreported distribution scheme.

relationship: Same-chapter the announced gifts specified by the full recipient catalogue
rationale: David sends spoils to Judah's elders and his neighbours; the following catalogue names the recipient groups through Hebron and all places his men passed, including the original 28a continuation without identifying uncertain place forms with another edition.

relationship: Same-chapter Beth-zur, southern Ramah and Jeththor as specified gift recipients

relationship: Same-chapter Aroer, Ammadi, Saphi and Esthie in the announced distribution
rationale: Aroer, the Ammadi, Saphi and Esthie specify a further recipient group under David's announced spoils gift; the introductory notice supplies sender and distribution purpose while the distinct place and group wording stays unchanged.

relationship: Same-chapter the preserved continuation names further spoils recipients
rationale: The continuation unit explicitly adds Gath, Kinan, Saphek and Thimath to the recipient catalogue introduced by David sending spoils to elders and neighbours; it remains a separate original unit without identifying its Gath with another passage's location.

relationship: Same-chapter Carmel and the Ierameli and Kenezi cities as recipients
rationale: Carmel, the Ierameli cities and the Kenezi cities are particular groups receiving the gifts announced to Judah's elders and David's neighbours, preserving those supplied collective forms without equating them to differently named peoples elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter Ierimouth, Beer-sheba and Noo in David's gift catalogue
rationale: Ierimouth, Beer-sheba and Noo specify another named recipient group within David's announced spoils distribution; the introduction supplies the gift's sender and intended elders-and-neighbours setting without resolving these names against other catalogues.

relationship: Same-chapter Hebron and the itinerary qualifier close the announced gift list
rationale: The catalogue ends with Hebron and all the places through which David and his men passed; its introduction states that David sent spoils to Judah's elders and his neighbours, preserving the closing itinerary qualifier without mapping every earlier name to a site.

relationship: Parallel opening account of Israel's defeat on Gelboue
rationale: Both accounts state that the foreigners fight Israel, Israel flees and men fall wounded on Mount Gelboue, matching the named combatants, retreat and supplied mountain form.

relationship: Parallel Saul-son death reports with the supplied name forms retained
rationale: Both report foreigners striking Saul's sons and explicitly name Jonathan; 1 Samuel supplies Aminadab and Melchisa, while Chronicles supplies Amminadab and Melchisoue, retaining those differences without certifying the proposed individual-name equivalences.

relationship: Parallel heavy battle and archers finding Saul
rationale: Both describe the battle growing heavy against Saul and archers finding him; 1 Samuel specifically places his wound beneath the ribs, whereas Chronicles describes suffering from the bows, keeping each account's injury wording.

relationship: Parallel sword request, frightened equipment carrier and Saul's sword fall
rationale: Both record Saul asking his equipment carrier to pierce him, the carrier refusing from fear and Saul falling on the sword; the additional piercing threat in 1 Samuel and the shared fear of mockery remain distinct supplied details.

relationship: Narrated sword fall compared with the Amalekite visitor's different account
rationale: The 1 Samuel account narrates the armour-bearer's refusal and Saul falling on the sword; the later visitor says Saul requested death and claims he himself killed him, preserving that reporting perspective without independently settling how the accounts relate.

relationship: Parallel equipment carrier's death after seeing Saul dead
rationale: Both accounts explicitly say the equipment carrier sees that Saul is dead and then falls on a sword and dies, preserving the stated observation and action rather than inferring it from the earlier request alone.

relationship: Parallel death summaries with different additional scope
rationale: Both summaries state Saul and his three sons die; 1 Samuel additionally names the armour-bearer and Chronicles says all his house died together, keeping those scopes distinct rather than asserting every biological descendant was killed.

relationship: Parallel abandoned cities and foreign settlement after the defeat
rationale: Both connect Israel's flight and the deaths of Saul and his sons with abandoned cities that the foreigners inhabit; 1 Samuel names the regions beyond the valley and Jordan, while Chronicles names those in the valley, retaining the different geographical scope.

relationship: Parallel following-day discovery of Saul and his sons on Gelboue
rationale: Both accounts place the discovery of fallen Saul and his sons on Gelboue on the following day; 1 Samuel describes stripping the dead and Chronicles plundering the wounded, preserving the actual objects of the looting description.

relationship: Parallel stripped equipment and announcements to idols and people
rationale: Both strip Saul's equipment and describe news announced through the foreigners' land to idols and people; Chronicles also explicitly mentions taking his head, a detail not added to the 1 Samuel unit.

relationship: Different stated displays of Saul's equipment and remains
rationale: 1 Samuel places the equipment in Astarte's temple and the body on Beth-shan's wall; Chronicles places equipment in their god's house and the head in Dagon's house, preserving the different objects and venues without supplying an unreported transfer.

relationship: Jabesh's hearing of Saul's fate recalls his earlier deliverance of that community
rationale: The inhabitants of Jabesh in Gilead hear what happened to Saul; the earlier account names Jabesh's promised deliverance and Saul's attack on the Ammonite camp, supplying the particular prior community connection without declaring an unreported motive for the later retrieval.

relationship: Parallel retrieval reports with differing bodies and treatment details
rationale: In 1 Samuel, the mighty men retrieve Saul and Jonathan from Beth-shan and burn them at Jabesh; Chronicles has mighty men from Galaad bring Saul and his sons to Jabis and bury their bones, keeping the different supplied extent, forms and burning detail.

relationship: David's later blessing explicitly acknowledges Saul and Jonathan's burial
rationale: The 1 Samuel account reports Jabesh's men retrieving Saul and Jonathan and taking them to Jabesh; David later blesses Jabesh's leaders for mercy shown by burying Saul and Jonathan, expressly recalling the named community's treatment of the two men.

relationship: Bones burial and seven-day fasting with distinct supplied burial descriptions
rationale: Both accounts describe burying the bones and fasting seven days; 1 Samuel specifies cultivated ground at Jabesh, whereas Chronicles specifies an oak at Jabis, retaining the different descriptions without independently resolving the place forms.
